title_en: Shanghai Kedi Paper Products Packaging Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau — dispute over order to pay comprehensive insurance fees for migrant workers
ruling_gist_en: Entities engaged in labor dispatch business shall be registered and established in accordance with the law. Where an employer enters into a labor service agreement with a company that has not been registered with the industry and commerce administration and does not possess the qualification for labor dispatch operation, and thereby forms a de facto labor relationship with the dispatched personnel, the employer shall pay comprehensive insurance premiums for them in accordance with the law; the agreement between the employer and a subject without the qualification to pay premiums cannot exempt the employer from its statutory obligation to pay.
keywords_en: Administrative; Labor security supervision; Social insurance premium collection; First instance; Basic People's Court; Shanghai; Legal person; State organ; Labor Contract Law; Interim Measures of Shanghai Municipality on Comprehensive Insurance for Migrant Workers; Regulations on Labor Security Supervision; Qualification recognition of labor dispatch units; Determination of de facto labor relationship; Exemption from statutory payment obligation; Dismissal of claims; Labor dispatch; Arrears of comprehensive insurance premiums; Unregistered with industry and commerce administration
full_text_en:
Shanghai Kedi Paper Products Packaging Co., Ltd. v. Shanghai Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security — dispute over an order to make up payments for comprehensive insurance for migrant workers

【Ruling Summary】

A unit engaged in labor dispatch business shall be established and registered in accordance with the law. Where an employer enters into an employment agreement with a company that has not undergone industrial and commercial registration and does not have the qualification for operating labor dispatch services, and a de facto labor relationship is formed between the employer and the dispatched personnel, the employer shall pay comprehensive insurance premiums for such personnel in accordance with the law. An agreement reached between the employer and a party that does not have the qualification to pay such premiums cannot exempt the employer from its statutory payment obligation.

Plaintiff: Shanghai Kedi Paper Products Packaging Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Li Xue Road, Malu Town, Jiading District, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Zhang Xianjun, Chairman of the Board of the company.

Defendant: Shanghai Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security, domiciled at: Zhongshan South Road, Shanghai.

Legal Representative: Zhou Haiyang, Director General of the Bureau.

The plaintiff, Shanghai Kedi Paper Products Packaging Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Kedi Company), dissatisfied with the administrative handling decision No. Hu Ren She Jian (2008) Li Zi No. 2221 made by the defendant, Shanghai Municipal Bureau of Human Resources and Social Security (hereinafter referred to as the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau), filed a lawsuit with the Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai.

The plaintiff, Kedi Company, alleged: When the labor supervision department subordinate to the defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, was investigating the plaintiff's alleged arrears of comprehensive insurance premiums for 72 migrant workers, the plaintiff explicitly informed it that 35 of those personnel were dispatched to the plaintiff by a third party, Shanghai Huangshi Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huangshi Company), under an agreement between the two parties, and were not employees of the plaintiff. Despite knowing this fact, the defendant nevertheless made an administrative handling decision requiring the plaintiff to pay comprehensive insurance premiums for 72 migrant workers totaling RMB 85,759.90. The plaintiff contends that the defendant's handling decision is unlawful and therefore requests the court to set aside the administrative handling decision No. Hu Ren She Jian (2008) Li Zi No. 2221 made by the defendant on January 6, 2009.

The defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, argued: As confirmed by the defendant's investigation, the 72 migrant workers specified in the administrative handling decision all worked at the plaintiff, Kedi Company, were managed by the plaintiff, and received their remuneration from the plaintiff. The plaintiff's assertion that 35 of those personnel were not its employees is untenable. The administrative handling decision made by the defendant is based on clear facts, solid evidence, lawful procedures, and correct applicable legal bases, and the defendant requests the court to uphold it.

During the trial, the defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, provided the following evidence to prove the facts found in the administrative handling decision: the Enterprise Legal Person Business License, the Organization Code Certificate, the Shanghai Labor and Social Security Inspection Registration Form; the Investigation Record made by the defendant against Zhang Xianjun, the plaintiff's legal representative, on November 6, 2008; the Factory-Wide Personnel List, the Attendance Assessment Form, the Employee Attendance Record Form, and the Payroll Form; the Rectification Report submitted by the plaintiff, Kedi Company; the Reply to the Entrusted Letter of Assistance with reference No. (Jiading) Wai Guan (2008) Hui Zi No. (022211) and its attached Detail of Personnel for Foreign Labor Insurance Payment; the agreement between the plaintiff and Shanghai Huangshi Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Huangshi Company"); the Employee Payment Status Table; and the Administrative Handling Decision No. Hu Ren She Jian (2008) Li Zi No. 2221. Among these, the Factory-Wide Personnel List, the Attendance Assessment Form, the Employee Attendance Record Form, and the Payroll Form showed that a total of 95 migrant workers received remuneration from the plaintiff's entity, were subject to the entity's daily management, and were all employees of the plaintiff. The agreement between the plaintiff and Huangshi Company was not affixed with an official seal, thus failing to meet the formal requirements of an agreement. Moreover, the defendant learned that Huangshi Company had neither industrial and commercial registration nor a social insurance account. Therefore, the defendant did not recognize the authenticity of the agreement.

The court conducted cross-examination in accordance with the law. The plaintiff, Kedi Company, raised objections to the evidence group consisting of the Factory-Wide Personnel List, the Attendance Assessment Form, the Employee Attendance Record Form, and the Payroll Form presented by the defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau. The plaintiff argued that all materials in this evidence group were temporarily filled in by the plaintiff at the request of the labor inspection personnel, and their contents were not truthful. The plaintiff further argued that the agreement between the plaintiff and Huangshi Company was true and valid, and Huangshi Company had dispatched 35 of its employees to work at the plaintiff company pursuant to the agreement. Therefore, the comprehensive insurance premiums for these workers should not be paid by the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not raise objections to the other evidence materials presented by the defendant.

The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai found the following facts at first instance:

The plaintiff, Kedi Company, is a limited liability company lawfully established and registered. On August 26, 2008, the defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, received a report indicating that the plaintiff had failed to pay comprehensive insurance premiums for the migrant workers it employed, among other issues. On September 17, September 25, and October 7 of the same year, the defendant issued Letters of Investigation and Inquiry to the plaintiff, conducting labor and social security supervision over the plaintiff. During this period, the plaintiff provided the defendant with materials including the *Factory-Wide Personnel List*, the *Attendance Assessment Form*, the *Employee Attendance Record Form*, and the *Payroll Form*. On November 5, 2008, the defendant initiated a case. After investigation, the defendant found that from March 2005 to October 2008, the plaintiff had failed to pay comprehensive insurance premiums for 95 migrant workers as required. Consequently, on November 6, 2008, the defendant served a Notice of Order to Make Corrections on the plaintiff, requiring the plaintiff to pay the overdue comprehensive insurance premiums for migrant workers before November 16, 2008. On November 19, 2008, the defendant sent a letter to the administrative department for migrant workers in Jiading District, requesting verification of the amount of comprehensive insurance premiums the plaintiff should make up. On December 10 of the same year, the Jiading District administrative department for migrant workers issued the *Reply to the Entrusted Letter of Assistance* along with the attached *Detail of Personnel for Foreign Labor Insurance Payment*, confirming that the plaintiff had not paid comprehensive insurance premiums for 72 migrant workers, including Wang Guoying, for the period from March 2005 to October 2008, totaling RMB 85,759.90. As the plaintiff did not implement corrective measures, the defendant on January 6, 2009, made the administrative handling decision No. Hu Ren She Jian (2008) Li Zi No. 2221, determining that Kedi Company's failure to pay comprehensive insurance premiums for 72 migrant workers, including Wang Guoying, during the period from March 2005 to October 2008, violated Articles 5 and 8 of the *Interim Measures of Shanghai Municipality on Comprehensive Insurance for Migrant Workers*. Pursuant to Article 19, Paragraph 2 of the said *Interim Measures*, the defendant issued an administrative handling decision requiring Kedi Company to pay, within fifteen days of receiving this decision, the comprehensive insurance premiums for the 72 migrant workers, including Wang Guoying, for the period from March 2005 to October 2008, totaling RMB 85,759.90. If not paid within the specified period, in addition to the arrears, a late payment penalty of 0.2% per day would be imposed from the due date. If the administrative handling decision was not implemented, a fine of RMB 2,000 to RMB 20,000 would be imposed pursuant to Article 30, Paragraph 1, Item (3) of the *Regulations on Labor and Social Security Supervision*. During the trial, the plaintiff did not dispute the fact found by the defendant that the 72 migrant workers, including Wang Guoying, had worked for the plaintiff from March 2005 to October 2008 and that no comprehensive insurance premiums had been paid for them during this period. The court accordingly confirmed the authenticity of this fact.

The issues in dispute at first instance were: whether some of the 72 migrant workers, including Wang Guoying, were dispatched by other companies; and whether the agreement between the plaintiff, Kedi Company, and the third party regarding the payment of comprehensive insurance premiums for this group of migrant workers could exempt the plaintiff from its payment obligation.

The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai held at first instance:

I. Regarding the dispute over whether some of the migrant workers were employees of the plaintiff, Kedi Company. The plaintiff claimed that some of the migrant workers were dispatched to the plaintiff by a third party, Huangshi Company, under an agreement between the two parties, and were not employees of the plaintiff. The plaintiff presented the agreement between itself and Huangshi Company. First, in terms of the content of the agreement, the two parties agreed that Huangshi Company would dispatch some workers to work at the plaintiff's entity for a period of one year, that these workers should enjoy equal treatment to the plaintiff's employees, and that the plaintiff's entity would periodically settle the wages of these workers. On its face, this agreement conforms to the content that a labor dispatch agreement under the *Labor Contract Law* should contain, and it also includes provisions regarding the payment of social insurance premiums for the dispatched workers. However, upon investigation and verification by the collegial panel, the agreement suffers from the defect that the subject party is not qualified. According to Article 57 of the *Labor Contract Law*: "A labor dispatch unit shall be established in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Company Law, and its registered capital shall not be less than RMB 500,000." Accordingly, a labor dispatch unit shall be a company lawfully registered and established, possessing a certain economic strength and capable of independently bearing legal liability. However, Huangshi Company was neither registered and established through industrial and commercial registration, nor did it have a registration account in the social insurance system, and there was no record of it having paid social insurance premiums for any worker. Although the plaintiff claimed to have examined Huangshi Company's industrial and commercial business license, it failed to provide it during the trial, and there was no other evidence to prove that Huangshi Company was an employer with the operational qualifications to lawfully dispatch labor services to the plaintiff. Therefore, in this case, Huangshi Company was not a lawfully established company and did not possess the legal qualifications for labor dispatch. Furthermore, a labor dispatch unit shall also conclude a labor contract for a term of not less than two years with the dispatched workers and pay them basic labor remuneration. However, in this case, the 35 migrant workers involved did not sign a labor contract with Huangshi Company, nor did they actually work at Huangshi Company. Instead, they had been working at the plaintiff's entity, performing the plaintiff's production tasks. Therefore, the labor dispatch relationship claimed by the plaintiff cannot be established.

Given that the labor dispatch relationship is not established, this case needs to determine whether the 35 migrant workers were employees of the plaintiff, Kedi Company, and consequently, whether the plaintiff should pay comprehensive insurance premiums for them. A labor relationship is a relationship between an employer and a worker. According to Article 16 of the *Labor Law*: "A labor contract is an agreement between a worker and an employer to establish a labor relationship and define the rights and obligations of both parties. A labor contract shall be concluded for the establishment of a labor relationship." Accordingly, the conclusion of a labor contract is the primary marker for establishing a labor relationship. However, in practice, many employers use workers without concluding labor contracts with them. For this reason, the 1995 Ministry of Labor's *Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the *Labor Law of the PRC** introduced the concept of a "de facto labor relationship." Article 1 of these Opinions states, "Where a labor relationship is formed between enterprises or individual economic organizations within the territory of China and workers, i.e., where a worker has in fact become a member of the enterprise or individual economic organization and has provided compensated labor, the *Labor Law* shall apply." The "de facto labor relationship" stipulated here is relative to the labor legal relationship regulated by the *Labor Law*. Although a worker and an employer have not signed a written labor contract, they have performed an actual labor relationship, including providing labor for the employer, accepting the employer's management and direction, receiving the employer's protection, etc., that is, the parties have in fact established a labor relationship. To protect the rights of workers in de facto labor relationships, the *Labor Contract Law of the PRC* further clarifies. Article 7 provides: "An employer shall establish a labor relationship with a worker from the date the employer starts using the worker." Article 10 provides: "To establish a labor relationship, a written labor contract shall be concluded. ... If an employer concludes a labor contract with a worker before using the worker, the labor relationship shall be established from the date of the start of the use of the worker." Accordingly, the basic legal fact that gives rise to a labor relationship is the use of the worker (the commencement of work), not the conclusion of a labor contract. As long as there is an act of using a worker, the worker enjoys the rights provided by law. Generally, the existence of a de facto labor relationship can be identified from the following four aspects: (1) Whether there is a relationship of subordination between the worker and the employer, where the worker accepts the employer's management, direction, and supervision; (2) Whether the employer organizes wage distribution according to some distribution principle, and whether the worker receives labor remuneration in a certain manner; (3) Whether the labor provided by the worker is part of the employer's business; (4) Whether the worker works in the workplace provided by the employer and uses the production tools provided by the employer. In the case of a labor dispatch, a labor relationship is formed between the labor dispatch unit and the dispatched worker. Applied to the facts of this case, since the labor dispatch relationship is not established, what needs to be examined is whether a de facto labor relationship existed between the plaintiff and the 35 migrant workers. From the series of evidence that underwent cross-examination at trial, the records made by the plaintiff during the labor supervision process can prove that the plaintiff's company used a total of 95 migrant workers, including the 35 disputed migrant workers. The evidence materials provided by the plaintiff, such as the attendance assessment form, the employee attendance record form, and the payroll form, also reflect that the plaintiff had a total of 95 employees, including this group of migrant workers, who all worked at the plaintiff's entity, performed the plaintiff's production tasks, were subject to the plaintiff's unified management, and received wages from the plaintiff. During the trial, the plaintiff also confirmed the fact that the 35 migrant workers worked at the plaintiff's entity. Accordingly, the relationship between this group of migrant workers and the plaintiff conforms to the basic characteristics of a de facto labor relationship. They should be considered employees of the plaintiff, and the plaintiff shall perform the relevant statutory obligations of an employer.

II. Regarding the dispute over whether the agreement between the plaintiff, Kedi Company, and the third party regarding the payment of comprehensive insurance premiums for some of the migrant workers could exempt the plaintiff from its payment obligation. In this case, the legal basis applied by the defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, in making the specific administrative act was the relevant provisions of the *Interim Measures of Shanghai Municipality on Comprehensive Insurance for Migrant Workers* (hereinafter referred to as the *Interim Measures*). The *Interim Measures* was formulated by the Shanghai Municipal Government to effectively address the social security issues of migrant workers, based on the characteristics and needs of migrant workers themselves. It plays an important role and has positive significance in safeguarding their lawful rights and providing norms for the employment practices of entities. The comprehensive insurance for migrant workers, as a form of social insurance, is compulsorily implemented by the government. All entities within the administrative area of this Municipality that employ migrant workers and the migrant workers they employ shall participate in accordance with the regulations. Under these Measures, the employer that uses migrant workers shall pay comprehensive insurance premiums for each migrant worker on a timely and full basis. This is not only an important means of lawfully safeguarding the lawful rights and interests of migrant workers and providing relief through pooled funds when migrant workers suffer work-related injuries, illnesses, or other accidents, but also an important method for employing entities to lawfully avoid employment risks and prevent labor disputes. The defendant found that the plaintiff failed to perform its statutory payment obligation based on Articles 5 and 8 of the *Interim Measures*, and made an administrative handling decision ordering the plaintiff to make up the overdue comprehensive insurance premiums. The plaintiff, however, argued that Article 5 of the agreement between the plaintiff and Huangshi Company stipulates: "The comprehensive insurance for workers shall be paid by Party A (i.e., Huangshi Company)." Therefore, Huangshi Company should bear the obligation to pay the comprehensive insurance premiums. Hence, the issue that needs to be clarified is: how to determine the entity obligated to pay comprehensive insurance premiums, and whether the agreement between the plaintiff and Huangshi Company can exclude the plaintiff's payment obligation.

According to Article 3 of the *Interim Measures*, enterprises, institutions, social organizations, and other entities that "use migrant workers" are collectively referred to as employers and are subject to these Measures. Article 5 stipulates the entities obligated to pay comprehensive insurance premiums, namely "employers and migrant workers without an employer." Article 8 further provides: "Employers and migrant workers without an employer shall, from the month of going through the comprehensive insurance registration formalities, pay comprehensive insurance premiums on a monthly basis to the municipal employment administration body for migrant workers." Accordingly, the employer that uses migrant workers is the statutory entity obligated to pay comprehensive insurance premiums for the period during which the migrant workers work for it. In the case of a legal labor dispatch relationship, the labor dispatch unit, as the statutory employer, qualifies as an "employer" under these Measures and shall bear the obligation to pay comprehensive insurance premiums. Since the labor dispatch relationship is not established in this case, and the plaintiff, being a corporate legal person with a lawful industrial and commercial registration and legitimate employer qualifications, actually used the migrant workers in this case and established a de facto labor relationship with them, it is the statutory payer under the *Interim Measures* and shall pay comprehensive insurance premiums for this group of migrant workers. As for the agreement between the plaintiff and Huangshi Company, because Huangshi Company does not possess lawful labor dispatch qualifications and is not a qualified entity capable of assuming the responsibility to pay comprehensive insurance premiums, the plaintiff's attempt to transfer its statutory payment obligation to a third party without payment qualifications through an agreement does not comply with the provisions of the *Interim Measures* and therefore cannot exempt the plaintiff from its payment obligation.

In conclusion, the administrative handling decision made by the defendant, the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, is based on clear facts and correct application of law. The reasons for the plaintiff Kedi Company's lawsuit are unfounded, and the court will not support its claims in accordance with the law.

Accordingly, the Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai, pursuant to Article 56, Item (4) of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the *Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC**, on May 27, 2009, rendered the following judgment:

The plaintiff Kedi Company's claims are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 50 (prepaid by the plaintiff Kedi Company) shall be borne by the plaintiff.

Kedi Company, dissatisfied with the above judgment, appealed to the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court. During the second instance proceedings, the court of second instance twice sent summonses for trial, on July 22 and August 19, 2009, to the address confirmed by the appellant, summoning the appellant to appear in court on August 6 and August 25, 2009. However, the appellant, after receiving the summonses, failed to appear in court without justifiable reasons. Accordingly, the Shanghai Second Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 48 of the *Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC* and Article 49, Paragraph 1 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the *Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC**, on August 26, 2009, rendered the following ruling:

This case is treated as a withdrawal of the appeal.

The appellate case acceptance fee of RMB 50 is reduced by half to RMB 25, to be borne by the appellant Kedi Company.

This ruling is final.
